input: the staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 18%, and the figure is defended here against the lower alternative put to the steering group. Essentially, a ramp set lower purchases its saving in the early months and pays for it later: the work packages that open the project are staffed by the same grades that close them, and a team assembled late inherits drawings, vendor data, and site knowledge that a team assembled on the ramp already holds. The 18% is a ramp rather than a level: staffing rises to the figure as the packages open and falls away as they close, so the cost of the ramp is carried for the execution period only. The shape is dictated by the sequence of the work itself. Mobilisation, detailed design, and procurement run in overlapping bands, and each band draws on the staff the previous band has brought in; a slower ramp starves the later bands at the point where their workload peaks, and the shortfall is then recovered, if it is recovered at all, by overtime and contract staff at rates the project does not control. The cost table in the Costs section carries the ramp as a single line against the alternatives, and the comparison there is the comparison the steering group is asked to accept: the saving from the lower figure is confined to the early period, while the exposure it creates sits in the execution period, where a staffing shortfall converts directly into delay. FID does not alter the argument, because the constraint is not the decision date but the hiring market for the grades in question, and a ramp written below what that market can deliver is a plan the project cannot staff against
